pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Understand ADDITION as combining or putting together two groups to find the total ('how many altogether'). One of the two conceptual roots of the whole domain (centrality 0.54) — every later strategy, fact, and algorithm rests on it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving addition (+)…'; 'solve one-step problems that involve addition… using concrete objects and pictorial representations'; non-statutory: 'this establishes addition and subtraction as related operations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 'represent addition… with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings…'; K.OA.2 solve add-to and put-together word problems; the two problem structures (add-to / put-together) are the canonical starting semantics.
• Operational details — Distinguish the two situations under 'combining': ADD-TO (a set grows: 3 here, 2 MORE arrive) and PUT-TOGETHER (two static parts seen as one whole). Model with physical objects the child physically pushes together, narrate the action, then attach the total. Cardinality (last-number-said = how many) is the hard prerequisite — the child must trust the count of the whole. Keep numbers within 5-10 and keep the ACTION visible before any symbol.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): physically combine two groups and re-count all to say the total. Tier B (age 5): act out an add-to story and state 'how many altogether' without prompting to recount from 1. Tier C (age 5-6): explain in words that addition means putting together to find the total, and match a combining situation to the idea of 'more/altogether'.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH combining semantics explicitly — add-to (dynamic: a group grows) and put-together (static: two parts, one whole) — because children who only meet 'and then more came' struggle with part-part-whole and missing-part problems later.
Move through concrete → pictorial → spoken before any + symbol: children push real objects together, then draw, then describe; the symbol (a separate topic) comes only once the ACTION is understood.
Narrate the action and the result separately ('3 and 2 more… that's 5 altogether') so 'altogether/total' becomes attached to the combined quantity, not just the last object counted.
Use fingers, ten-frames and story contexts children act out, so addition is a thing you DO to quantities, not a written procedure to memorise.
Build on secure cardinality: if a child recounts the whole from 1 every time, that is expected early — encourage but do not force 'counting on' until counting-all is fluent.
keyRepresentations: Two groups of physical objects (counters, cubes, toys) that are literally pushed together
Ten-frame(s) filling up as objects are added
Part-part-whole (part-whole 'cherry') model showing two parts joining into a whole
Fingers and five-frames for small totals
Story/act-out situations and simple drawings of an add-to or put-together scene
commonMisconceptions: Recounting the whole from 1 every time and never trusting the total — a cardinality gap surfacing inside addition.
Thinking addition always means 'a group gets bigger by things arriving' (add-to only), so static put-together and part-part-whole situations aren't recognised as addition.
Believing the total is 'the last number you say' regardless of combining, i.e. reciting rather than combining quantities.
Losing track when combining by miscounting the join (double-counting an object or skipping one).
Assuming the bigger group must be said/written first, an early seed of not seeing addition as flexible (commutativity comes later).

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Year 1): understand ADDITION as combining or putting together two groups to find the total ('how many altogether'). Teach both combining meanings explicitly — ADD-TO (a group grows: 3 here, 2 MORE arrive) and PUT-TOGETHER (two static parts seen as one whole). Keep the physical ACTION of joining visible before any written symbol, build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many), and attach the words 'altogether/total' to the whole combined set. Keep numbers small (within 5-10).

activities.title: Combining mat: push two groups into one whole
feedback: If the child names just one group as the total (e.g. says 3): physically push the groups together and count the single combined set with them; contrast 'how many red?' with 'how many altogether?' so the merging is felt. An optional live total counter that climbs 3→4→5 as the piles merge makes the whole-set count visible.

If the child re-counts the whole pile from one every time: this is a normal early stage — do not mark it wrong and do not drill. Keep modelling 'hold 3 in your head... 4, 5' and counting-on emerges as cardinality matures.
If the method is right but the final count slips to 4 or 6: scaffold one-to-one counting by moving each counter aside as it is counted; the combining idea is intact, so do not reteach the concept.
Reinforce by asking the child to re-count the whole and confirm the total is the whole set, not the last object touched.
activities.rationale: Addition-as-combining is an action on quantities; letting the child drag two groups together and watch a single total emerge from their own action is intended to make 'two parts become one countable whole' concrete. Concrete action precedes pictorial and symbolic work, and both add-to and put-together structures are the canonical starting semantics. A live recomputing total and mode toggle are optional supports that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms. This is a proposed activity, not an empirically validated one.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images and drawings; solve add-to and put-together word problems within 10.
The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.

Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving + and solve one-step addition problems with concrete objects and pictorial representations; addition and subtraction are established as related operations.
learnerActions: Drop three counters into one framed region (a basket or ten-frame) and two counters into a second framed region beside it.
Count each part aloud: 'three red here, two blue here.'
Physically sweep both piles together into a single large 'altogether' region.
Count the whole merged set and say how many there are altogether.
Say the matching sentence aloud: 'three and two more — that's five altogether.' (Leave the written 3 + 2 = 5 for the later, separate symbol topic.)
Switch modes: in ADD-TO, add objects to one existing group one at a time ('3... then 2 more arrive'); in PUT-TOGETHER, start with two ready-made parts and merge them at once.
activities.intendedInsight: Two separate groups the child made become ONE group with a single count — addition felt as a physical join, not a recited fact. 'Altogether' names the whole combined set, however it was built.

activities.title: Act out an add-to story
feedback: If the child only counts the arrivals or only the starting group, replay the story slowly and count everyone present at the end together.
Praise retelling that keeps the action ('and then more came') and the result ('altogether') distinct.
activities.rationale: Children who only meet 'and then more came' can struggle with part-part-whole later, and children who only meet static parts may not recognise growth as addition; acting out add-to stories is intended to secure the dynamic meaning. Story contexts children act out are intended to make addition something the child does to quantities. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images and drawings; solve add-to and put-together word problems within 10.
The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.
learnerActions: Act out a situation with real children or toys: e.g. 3 children are on the mat, then 2 more join.
Narrate the action and the result separately: '3 children... then 2 more came... that's 5 altogether.'
State 'how many altogether' after the join without being told to recount from one.
Retell the story using fingers or a five-/ten-frame to show the growing group.
activities.intendedInsight: Add-to situations (a group grows as more arrive) are a form of addition, and the total names the whole group after the new members join.

activities.title: Part-part-whole picture scene and 'altogether?' flap
feedback: If the child gives a subset (e.g. 3): point to each group in turn, then sweep a hand around the whole scene and count everyone.
Use the part-whole diagram to show both parts belong inside one whole.
activities.rationale: A static scene is a clean anchor for the put-together idea and the word 'altogether', but it shows a finished sum rather than letting the child perform the join — so it labels the act more than it builds it. Use it as a scaffold alongside hands-on combining, not as the sole route.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images and drawings; solve add-to and put-together word problems within 10.
The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.
learnerActions: Look at a static scene with two groups (e.g. 3 ducks on the bank, 2 ducks in the water).
Count each group by pointing to it.
Answer 'how many altogether?' and then check by lifting a flap or revealing the total.
Fit the two parts into a part-whole ('cherry') diagram: two parts joining into one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Two static parts can be seen together as one whole — the put-together meaning of addition — even when nothing is moving or arriving.

activities.title: Talk it through while combining
feedback: Accept gestures and object-moves as valid explanations at this age; the child's language is still forming.

If the child insists the bigger group must come first, let them combine in both orders and count — they should find the same total (an informal, early seed of commutativity, which is formalised later).
activities.rationale: Dialogue can elicit a young child's thinking and may reveal whether they treat two groups as one total, but the concept is fundamentally about acting on objects, so talk should sit alongside manipulables rather than replace them. Noticing order-independence here is an early, informal seed (formal commutativity comes later).
learnerActions: Alongside real objects, respond to a warm prompt: 'Let's put these together — how many now?'
Explain in words what 'altogether' means by showing it with the counters.
Answer probing questions: 'If I add the blue ones to the red ones instead of red to blue, do we still get 5? Why?' and 'What if there were 3 red and 4 blue — how many altogether?'
If a pretend friend says the answer is 3, explain what you would tell them.
activities.intendedInsight: A child can articulate that addition means combining to find how many altogether, and begins to notice the order of combining doesn't change the total.

constraints: Keep numbers within 5-10 and keep the joining action visible before introducing the + symbol; the written symbol is a later, separate topic.
Build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many). If the child cannot trust the count of the whole, that prerequisite needs attention before counting-on is expected.
Counting-all from one is an expected early developmental stage — encourage but do not force 'counting on', and do not mark counting-all as wrong.
Picture-only scenes and lift-the-flap totals are scaffolds for the 'altogether' label; they do not let the child perform the combining and should not be the only experience.

A scored multiple-choice/linear check may test recognition of a combined total but does not itself elicit the child's physical combining or spoken explanation, and such assessment is developmentally weak at ages 4-6; keep any such check to picture-based items with very small numbers and never as the main activity.

On-screen 3D manipulation (rotating or positioning virtual 3D objects) adds handling cost for pre-readers without a clear conceptual gain here (combining small groups has little spatial payoff), so flat on-screen objects/scenes and real physical counters are preferred for this topic; this is a scoped judgement, not a claim that 3D never helps.
Teach both add-to and put-together explicitly so children recognise static part-part-whole situations as addition too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M and NCETM claims are marked unverified. Do not treat citations as evidence that these specific activities were tested.

The source's stated correct answer prefers 'counting on from the larger group', while its own guidance says counting-all is normal and should not be drilled at this age. These are consistent if 'counting on' is treated as the maturing goal, not the required method for ages 4-6; activities present counting-all as acceptable and counting-on as emerging.
The 'live total counter', mode toggle, drag-and-sweep, and lift-the-flap are retained as optional interaction/feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms.

The original pedagogy listed age-tiered Checkpoint expectations (Tier A ~age 4: combine and re-count all; Tier B ~age 5: act out an add-to story and state 'altogether' without prompting to recount; Tier C ~age 5-6: explain in words that addition means putting together). These are distributed across the three activities here rather than presented as explicit age-banded milestones; reconstruct the tier mapping if age-specific checks are needed.

probeDeeper: If I add the blue ones to the red ones instead of red to blue, do we still get 5? Why?
What if there were 3 red and 4 blue — how many altogether?
Show me with the counters what 'altogether' means.
A friend says the answer is 3. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 5 — found by combining the two groups into one, ideally counting ON from the larger group ('3 … 4, 5') or just knowing 3 and 2 make 5, rather than recounting every counter from one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts ALL from one every time — cannot hold the first quantity and count on, so recounts the whole merged pile from 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill counting-on or mark counting-all as wrong — it is a normal developmental stage that matures with cardinality; keep modelling 'hold 3 in your head, count on' and it emerges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child re-counts every counter from one rather than counting on from 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names one visible group as the total — answers 3 (or 2), treating 'altogether' as relabelling a group rather than merging both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically push the groups together and count the single combined set; contrast 'how many red' with 'how many altogether' so combining is felt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a subset count (3 or 2) as the total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines correctly but miscounts the merged pile (double-counts or skips a counter).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold one-to-one by moving each counter as it is counted; the combining concept is intact, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method is right (counts on / merges) but the final count slips to 4 or 6.

responseLevels.gap: Names one group as the total, or cannot find the total without recounting from one and still errs.
responseLevels.full: Treats the two groups as one total, counts on from the larger or recalls the fact, and explains that combining finds how many altogether.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 5 reliably but only by counting all from one; does not yet count on or recall, and combining is procedure-bound.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. If I put them together, how many are there altogether? How did you work it out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The number 5 alone does not reveal understanding; the METHOD and reason do. A child who grasps addition as combining treats the two groups as one merged total and counts on or recalls; a child who does not may name one of the groups as the answer, or must always recount the whole set from one. Asking 'how did you work it out' exposes which.
